title: Filling the Holy City: One in Ten Moves to Jerusalem
summary: To repopulate Jerusalem, the leaders settle there and the rest of the people cast lots to bring one family in ten into the city, while the others stay in their towns; volunteers are blessed for choosing to live in Jerusalem. The chapter lists the leading residents of the city from Judah, Benjamin, the priests, the Levites, and the gatekeepers, with their officers and numbers, and then names the towns and villages of Judah and Benjamin where the rest of the people lived.
story: Chapter 7 left Jerusalem walled but nearly empty: “the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it” (7:4). Nehemiah began then to enroll the people, but the story paused for the reading of the Law, the confession, and the covenant pledge of chapters 8 to 10. Now it picks up where chapter 7 left off. A walled city needs residents to defend it, to maintain the temple, and to make it a real capital again. This chapter completes that task, and chapter 12 will celebrate the dedication of the wall with a city that is finally inhabited.
historical:
Jerusalem in the Persian period was far smaller than it had been before 587/586 BC, and archaeology suggests the settled area was largely confined to the eastern ridge, the old City of David, and the temple mount. Many returnees preferred to live in the towns and villages where they had land, since farming was their livelihood and Jerusalem had few houses and little economic life apart from the temple. Moving into the capital meant giving up property and security for the sake of the city.

The list of residents has a close parallel in 1 Chronicles 9:2-34, with many of the same names but also differences, which suggests both drew on temple and civic records of the period. Verse 23 mentions a command from the king regulating the singers; interpreters are divided over whether this means the Persian king, who might have granted support to the temple staff (compare Ezra 7:24), or David, who is credited elsewhere with organizing the singers (12:24, 45-46). Verse 24 describes Pethahiah as the king's agent in matters concerning the people, which most take to mean a Jewish official who represented the community's affairs to the Persian court.
cultural:
Casting lots was a common way in Israel of making decisions that no one wanted to make by personal preference, and it was understood that God directed the result (Proverbs 16:33). The land itself had been divided among the tribes by lot (Joshua 14:2). Using lots to choose who would move into Jerusalem took the decision out of the hands of the powerful and treated it as God's allocation. Taking one in ten echoes the principle of the tithe, the tenth of produce given to God, and some interpreters see the people giving a tenth of their families to the holy city in the same spirit.

The towns listed in verses 25-35 include places with deep roots in Israel's history: Kiriath-arba (the old name of Hebron), Beersheba, Ziklag, Lachish, Azekah, Anathoth, Bethel, and Ramah. The description of settlement from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom (verse 30) echoes older descriptions of Judah's extent. Some scholars think the list describes where Jews actually lived, including areas beyond the official borders of the Persian province, while others think it expresses the community's claim to the old tribal territory.
literary: The chapter opens with a brief narrative (verses 1-2) and then gives two lists. The first (verses 3-24) names those who lived in Jerusalem, arranged by group: Judah (4-6), Benjamin (7-9), priests (10-14), Levites (15-18), gatekeepers (19), with notes on the temple servants, the overseer of the Levites, and the king's agent (20-24). Genealogies trace some leaders back several generations, and numbers are given for each group. The second list (verses 25-36) names the settlements outside Jerusalem, first of Judah and then of Benjamin. The holy city is named at the start and in the middle (verses 1 and 18), marking what the whole arrangement is for.

outline.t: Lots are cast and volunteers are blessed
Residents of Jerusalem from Judah and Benjamin
Temple servants, the singers' overseer, and the king's agent
The towns of Benjamin and the Levites' settlement

doctrines.note: Jerusalem is called “the holy city” (verses 1 and 18). The city is holy because God's temple is there. Living in it was an act of devotion as well as civic duty.
The use of lots entrusts the choice of who moves to God's direction. Personal preference, wealth, and influence are set aside in favor of a process the community believed God governed.
The residents listed are not only priests and Levites but also laymen, gatekeepers, and temple servants. The life of the holy city depended on the whole people, each group doing its part.

words.note: Nadav, to be willing or to volunteer. The same verb describes freewill offerings given without compulsion (as in Exodus 35:29). In verse 2 the people bless those who volunteered to live in Jerusalem, treating their move as a kind of offering.

Goral, lot. The word refers to the small stones or marked objects used to reach a decision, and it can also mean the portion or destiny assigned by lot. Here it chooses the families who will live in the city (verse 1).

Qodesh, holiness. In the phrase “the holy city” it describes Jerusalem as set apart for God. The prophets had promised that Jerusalem would again be called holy (Isaiah 52:1; Joel 3:17), and this chapter shows the promise taking a first, modest shape.

Paqid, overseer or officer. The word describes men appointed over groups within the city (verses 9, 14, 22). The repeated mention of overseers shows the resettled city being organized under responsible leadership.

christ: The link here is thematic. Jerusalem, the holy city repopulated in this chapter, is the city where Jesus would later teach, be crucified, rise again, and send his Spirit on the church at Pentecost. The New Testament also looks beyond the earthly Jerusalem to a heavenly one. Hebrews speaks of believers coming to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), and Revelation closes with the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God, a city whose residents are those written in the Lamb's book of life (Revelation 21:2, 27). The willingness of those in Nehemiah's day to leave their property to live in the holy city finds an echo in Hebrews 11:13-16, which describes the faithful as seeking a better, heavenly country.
questions: The people blessed those who volunteered to move to Jerusalem, because it was a sacrifice. What sacrifices have others made for the good of your community?
Casting lots removed personal advantage from the decision about who would move. How do you make decisions where your own interests are at stake?
Most of the chapter is names and places. Why might it matter to God, and to the writer, that ordinary residents and small villages were recorded?
